content: The systematic reviews conducted at PROSPERO provided detailed information about the methodologies employed, including the search strategies. These details are documented under each respective section in Chapter 3. Among these reviews, qualitative and cost analyses were performed for each topic, focusing on the values and preferences of end users, potential end users, and health workers in relation to the self-care interventions addressed by each PICO question. Evidence from nine systematic reviews was used to support six new recommendations and three key considerations, as summarized in GRADE tables. These tables provide the evidence base on effectiveness that informed the new recommendations in this guideline. Key considerations were developed for PICO questions where the Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that there was insufficient evidence to make a recommendation. For these issues, the GDG provided critical considerations that need to be addressed before future decisions can be made regarding the development of recommendations for these PICO questions. The four PICO questions that resulted in key considerations were as follows: 1. Should self-testing for proteinuria during pregnancy be available in addition to clinic check-ups? 2. Should pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) initiation be available following screening by a pharmacist, without a prescription? 3. Should PrEP continuation be available from a pharmacist, without a prescription? 4. Should self-administration of gender-affirming hormones be made available in addition to health worker administration? Discussions related to PICO questions 2 and 3, concerning PrEP initiation and continuation, were grouped into one set of key considerations. The World Health Organization (WHO) Department of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research conducted a scoping review of self-care definitions available in WHO tools and guidance. An initial search in the WHO Institutional Repository for Information Sharing (IRIS) for self-care retrieved 1,700 documents. After narrowing the focus to specific mentions of self-care, 922 WHO documents remained. These were categorized by year and topic in Microsoft Excel. After excluding documents that lacked clear definitions or explanatory narratives for self-care, 106 documents were reviewed. Three reviewers, including members of the systematic review teams, independently identified major themes across the definitions using qualitative coding and selected their top five definitions. They then discussed their findings to reach a consensus on a working definition for this guideline. The working definition for self-care in this guideline is derived from a 2009 WHO regional working group in South-East Asia. It defines self-care in the context of primary health care as the ability of individuals, families, and communities to promote health, prevent disease, maintain health, and cope with illness and disability with or without the support of a health worker. Self-care is a broad concept encompassing hygiene (both general and personal), nutrition (type and quality of food consumed), lifestyle (sporting activities, leisure, etc.), environmental factors (living conditions, social habits, etc.), socioeconomic factors (income level, cultural beliefs, etc.), and self-medication. Other common definitions of self-care in WHO documents include: Non-professional care, described as unorganized health activities and health-related decision-making by individuals, families, neighbors, friends, and colleagues at work. Self-care as the primary health resource within the health system, including informal health activities, self-medication, self-treatment, social support during illness, and first aid. Key aspects of self-care definitions include its relationship with the health system. Some definitions describe self-care as independent of or in opposition to the health system, while others view it as collaborative with or part of the health system. Self-care is often considered a component of primary health care, the first level of care, or a domain of the health system. Many definitions emphasize that self-care complements rather than substitutes for the health system, highlighting the co-production of care. Self-care is also described as essential to and simultaneous with the health system, representing a co-occurring phenomenon. Most definitions of self-care identify specific agents, usually non-health-care professionals, such as individuals, family members, or community structures. Self-care is typically located at home or in natural settings, reflecting the normal context of people's everyday lives. Definitions also describe the role of the health system in supporting self-care through information, technology, and techniques, or emphasize the need for linkage to or support from the health system, especially when describing self-care as part of a continuum. The scope of self-care definitions can generally be categorized into two dichotomies: habits or activities of daily living/lifestyle, and the management of illness, medications, or disease episodes. Some definitions relate self-care to coping, social support, or the emotional aspects of health management. In all cases, self-care involves active engagement, with individuals actively monitoring and responding to a changing environment. One WHO document defines self-care as an active, responsive, and flexible process of self-management. Individuals engaged in self-care are willing, capable, informed, and ready to take action for their own health. The working definition of self-care for this guideline is: The ability of individuals, families, and communities to promote health, prevent disease, maintain health, and cope with illness and disability with or without the support of a health worker. The scope of self-care in this definition includes health promotion, disease prevention and control, self-medication, providing care to dependents, seeking hospital/specialist care if needed, and rehabilitation, including palliative care. This concept recognizes that while various factors and processes influence behavior, it is ultimately the individual who acts (or does not act) to preserve health or respond to symptoms.
